tool_arguments.query: Super Micro Computer Q1 fiscal 2026 AI GPU server revenue breakdown percentage

trajectory.content: Super Micro Computer Q1 fiscal 2026 AI GPU server revenue breakdown percentage

Super Micro Computer (SMCI) did **not separately disclose an “AI server revenue” dollar line item** in its Q3 fiscal 2026 release; therefore, the reported company-wide net-sales figure is the definitive quarterly revenue measure. [[1]] 

For the fiscal third quarter ended **March 31, 2026**, Supermicro reported net sales of **$10.243 billion**, up **123% year over year** from **$4.600 billion** in Q3 FY2025 and down about **19% sequentially** from **$12.7 billion** in Q2 FY2026. [[1]] 

AI-related platforms reportedly represented **more than 90% of revenue in recent quarters**, which would imply an AI-platform revenue run rate of **more than roughly $9.2 billion** when applied to Q3’s $10.243 billion total; however, that is an inference rather than a company-reported Q3 AI-server-revenue figure. [[2]] [[1]] 

Other Q3 FY2026 results were **GAAP net income of $483 million**, **GAAP diluted EPS of $0.72**, **non-GAAP diluted EPS of $0.84**, and **GAAP gross margin of 9.9%**. [[1]] 

Management attributed the quarterly revenue shortfall versus its prior quarter to customer data-center/site-readiness delays and industry-wide supply constraints, while indicating that it expected delayed revenue to be recognized in subsequent quarters. [[3]] [[4]] 

For Q4 FY2026, Supermicro guided to **$11.0 billion–$12.5 billion** of net sales and maintained FY2026 net-sales guidance of **$38.9 billion–$40.4 billion**. [[1]]

[[1, 2]] 
The available analyst consensus was **$2.618 billion**, about **$43 million (1.7%) above** the high end of management’s range and **2.7% above** its midpoint, implying the principal near-term revenue-execution risk was expectations above formal guidance. [[3, 2]]

**Why AI demand appears material:** In Q2, Equinix said AI infrastructure demand was accelerating and that the vast majority of its largest deals were AI-workload driven; management characterized the demand as spanning private AI stacks, sovereign deployments, batch training/inference, and latency-sensitive inference. [[4]] 
This is not solely a hyperscaler-compute story: Equinix’s differentiated proposition is neutral, connected infrastructure, and the company stated that eight of the top 10 AI model providers and eight of the top 10 neoclouds use its platform for key networking workloads. [[4]]

**xScale leasing read-through:** The clearest quantitative evidence is **134 MW of xScale leasing signed across the Americas in Q2 2026**; its xScale portfolio totaled **604 MW leased**, with approximately **2,000 MW of capacity when fully built out** and more than **$23 billion** of total investment. [[5]] 
That leasing was financially consequential: Q2 revenue was **$2.625 billion**, up **16% year over year**, and management explicitly attributed part of that growth to one-time xScale fees; the Hampton xScale transaction alone contributed about **$120 million** of non-recurring fees. [[2, 6]] 
Accordingly, xScale validates substantial AI/hyperscale demand and supports future capacity utilization, but investors should distinguish recurring underlying demand from the timing volatility created by non-recurring leasing fees. [[2, 6]]

tool_arguments.query: Equinix Q2 2026 revenue $2.625 billion YoY growth details xScale non-recurring fees

trajectory.content: Equinix Q2 2026 revenue $2.625 billion YoY growth details xScale non-recurring fees

Equinix reported Q2 2026 revenue of **$2.625 billion** for the quarter ended June 30, 2026, up **16% year over year** on both a reported and normalized constant-currency basis. [[1]] 

The headline growth included both strong underlying demand and one-time xScale fees: recurring revenue was **$2.377 billion**, versus **$2.143 billion** a year earlier, while non-recurring revenue rose to **$248 million** from **$113 million**. [[1]] 

Thus, recurring revenue grew about **10.9% YoY**, indicating that most of the underlying growth remained robust even excluding the unusually large non-recurring contribution. [[1]] 

AI demand appears to be a meaningful operational driver rather than merely a narrative: annualized gross bookings increased **23% YoY**, backlog reached a record, and Equinix added a record **9,700 net interconnections** in the quarter. [[2]] 

Management said customer demand was broad-based and growing, and specifically positioned Equinix to serve enterprise networking, cloud, and AI-infrastructure requirements. [[2]] 

The key analytical caveat is that the **16%** total-revenue growth rate should not be treated as fully recurring, because the company explicitly attributed part of it to one-time xScale fees; the recurring-revenue trajectory and bookings/interconnection metrics are cleaner indicators of sustained AI-led demand. trajectory.content: Equinix dividend per share and REIT payout policy FY 2025 Q2

**FY2025 Q2 dividend per share:** Equinix paid a quarterly common-stock cash dividend of **$4.69 per share**, paid on **June 18, 2025** to shareholders of record on **May 21, 2025**. [[1]]

**REIT payout policy:** In its Q2 2025 Form 10-Q, Equinix stated that it expected its **2025 quarterly and other applicable distributions to equal or exceed REIT taxable income recognized in 2025**. [[2]] Equinix elected REIT tax status beginning in 2015; dividends paid are generally deductible against taxable income of the REIT and qualified REIT subsidiaries, while taxable REIT subsidiaries remain subject to corporate income tax. [[1]] 

Thus, the relevant policy is not a fixed percentage of GAAP earnings or AFFO; it is to distribute at least its REIT taxable income—consistent with maintaining REIT qualification—with the company indicating an intention to distribute the entire taxable income generated by its REIT and qualified REIT subsidiaries for 2025. [[1]]

Related coverage:
**Equinix (EQIX) dividend:** the current quarterly common-stock dividend is **$5.16 per share**, a 10% increase, payable March 18, 2026 to shareholders of record February 25, 2026. [[1]] 
Annualizing that rate implies **$20.64 per share**, subject to future board declarations. [[1]] 

For comparison, Equinix distributed **$4.69 per share per quarter**, or **$18.76 annualized**, during 2025. [[2]]

**REIT payout:** a REIT must distribute at least **90% of REIT taxable income**—calculated before the dividends-paid deduction and excluding net capital gains—to preserve REIT qualification; this is a tax-income test, not an AFFO payout-ratio target. [[3]] [[4]] 

Using Equinix’s 2026 guidance, expected cash dividends of approximately **$2.036 billion** represent about **48.0%–49.0% of guided AFFO** of $4.158–$4.238 billion; on a per-share basis, the $20.64 annualized dividend is about **48.3%–49.2%** of guided diluted AFFO per share of $41.93–$42.74. [[5]] 

Thus, Equinix’s cash dividend is roughly a **48%–49% AFFO payout**, while its legally required REIT distribution percentage is measured against taxable income and is at least 90%. [[5]] [[3]]

Arm Holdings’ Q3 FY2026 covered the quarter ended December 31, 2025, and total revenue was a record $1.242 billion, up 26% year over year. [[1]]

- **Royalty revenue:** **$737 million**, up **27%** from $580 million in Q3 FY2025. Arm attributed the increase to adoption of higher-royalty technologies—including Armv9 and Arm Compute Subsystems (CSS)—and increased use of Arm-based chips in data centers. [[1]]
- **License and other revenue:** **$505 million**, up **25%** from $403 million a year earlier, reflecting high-value licenses for next-generation Arm technologies; licensing revenue can also fluctuate with contract timing. [[1]]
- **Neoverse/data-center indicators:** Arm stated that Neoverse CPUs had exceeded **1 billion deployed cores** and that its share among top hyperscalers was expected to approach **50%**. [[2]]
- **Illustrative adoption:** AWS introduced fifth-generation Graviton using **Neoverse CSS V3** with **192 cores**, double Graviton4’s core count. [[2]] 

The key investment takeaway is that Q3 royalty growth was not solely shipment-volume-led: Arm specifically linked the 27% increase to a richer product mix and higher royalty per chip from Armv9/CSS, alongside expanding data-center deployment. [[1]]

- Scale-out-switch revenue is forecast to exceed **$600 million in FY2027**, about double year over year, with a path to approximately **$1 billion in FY2028**. [[2]]

- Marvell guided Q2 FY2027 revenue to **$2.700 billion ±5%** at the midpoint, or roughly **35% year-over-year growth**. [[4]]

trajectory.content: Marvell FY2026 full year data center revenue custom AI silicon electro-optics

**Marvell Technology — Q2 FY2026 (quarter ended August 2, 2025):** total revenue reached a record **$2.006 billion**, up **58% year over year** and **6% sequentially**; GAAP diluted EPS was **$0.22** and non-GAAP diluted EPS was **$0.67**. [[1]]

**Data center was the core growth engine:** revenue was **$1.491 billion**, representing **74% of company revenue**, up **69% year over year** and **3% sequentially** from $1.441 billion in Q1 FY2026. [[2]]

**Custom AI silicon and electro-optics:** management identified strong AI demand for these two product categories as a principal driver of the quarter’s growth, and stated that custom-AI design activity had reached an all-time high, with **more than 50 new opportunities across more than 10 customers**. [[2, 3]] 

Marvell did **not** disclose separate Q2 revenue amounts for custom AI silicon versus electro-optics; rather, it stated on the earnings call that the two product lines together accounted for **more than three quarters of data-center revenue**, implying more than roughly **$1.1 billion** of the $1.491 billion data-center total. [[4, 2]] 

For Q3 FY2026, Marvell guided total revenue to **$2.060 billion ±5%**; management expected overall data-center revenue to be approximately flat sequentially, as electro-optics strength offsets a near-term decline in custom revenue, while expecting custom-business growth to become substantially stronger in Q4. [[2, 4]]

**Bottom line:** Q2 demonstrated that Marvell’s AI exposure is already highly material—data center supplied nearly three quarters of revenue and its custom/optical franchises comprised the majority of that segment—but the Q3 outlook also illustrates that custom-silicon ramps can be nonlinear and customer-program timing can create quarterly volatility. [[2, 4]]

AWS revenue was $42.232 billion, up 37% year over year, while AWS operating income was $16.621 billion versus $10.160 billion a year earlier; the implied/reported segment operating margin was 39.4%. [[1]] [[2]]

**AI contribution:** Amazon did not disclose a separate quarterly dollar revenue or operating-profit contribution from AI within AWS. [[1]] [[2]] Net income of $62.6 billion included **$53.4 billion of non-operating pre-tax other income**, primarily related to Amazon’s Anthropic investment, so that gain should not be interpreted as AWS operating performance or recurring AI operating profit. Super Micro Computer (SMCI) did **not separately disclose an “AI server revenue” dollar line item** in its Q3 fiscal 2026 release; therefore, the reported company-wide net-sales figure is the definitive quarterly revenue measure. [[1]]

AI-related platforms reportedly represented **more than 90% of revenue in recent quarters**, which would imply an AI-platform revenue run rate of **more than roughly $9.2 billion** when applied to Q3’s $10.243 billion total; however, that is an inference rather than a company-reported Q3 AI-server-revenue figure. [[2]] [[1]]

Management attributed the quarterly revenue shortfall versus its prior quarter to customer data-center/site-readiness delays and industry-wide supply constraints, while indicating that it expected delayed revenue to be recognized in subsequent quarters. [[3]] [[4]] 

For Q4 FY2026, Supermicro guided to **$11.0 billion–$12.5 billion** of net sales and maintained FY2026 net-sales guidance of **$38.9 billion–$40.4 billion**. [[1]]

tool_arguments.query: Marvell Technology custom AI silicon electro-optics data center revenue split Q1 fiscal 2026

trajectory.content: Marvell Technology custom AI silicon electro-optics data center revenue split Q1 fiscal 2026

Marvell did **not disclose a Q1 FY2026 revenue split between custom AI silicon and electro-optics**, so an exact dollar or percentage allocation cannot be reliably calculated from its reported results. [[1]] 

The company reported **$1.4406 billion** of data-center revenue for the quarter ended **May 3, 2025**, equal to **76% of total company revenue**, with total revenue of **$1.895 billion**. [[1]] 

Management attributed data-center momentum to both the rapid scaling of custom-silicon programs and robust electro-optics shipments, but provided no component-level revenue figures or mix percentages for either category. [[1]] 

Thus, the defensible Q1 FY2026 “split” is: **Data center: $1.441 billion; custom AI silicon: not separately disclosed; electro-optics: not separately disclosed; residual data-center products: also not separately disclosed.** [[1]] 

Qualitatively, management indicated that its lead hyperscaler XPU program had become a key custom-business revenue driver and that optics was performing well and expected to grow during the year, but these comments do not establish a quarterly revenue mix. [[2]]

Sources:

| Other data-center products—e.g., switching, storage, and remaining interconnect | **Roughly 25%**, implying **about ~$1.5 billion-plus** |

Marvell’s own proxy describes optical interconnect as “roughly half” of FY2026 data-center revenue and custom silicon as “approximately 25%”; therefore, these are management-reported mix percentages rather than a formally disclosed, exact audited product-revenue table. [[3]] 

The custom-silicon figure is the clearest absolute disclosure: management said custom revenue doubled year over year to **$1.5 billion** in FY2026. [[2]] 

Accordingly, the practical FY2026 **custom silicon vs. optics split** is approximately **$1.5 billion custom / >$3.0 billion optics**, or about **25% / 50%** of the data-center business, respectively. [[3]]

trajectory.content: Arm Holdings Q3 fiscal 2026 royalty and licensing revenue data-center Neoverse

Arm Holdings’ fiscal Q3 2026 ended **December 31, 2025** and produced record revenue of **$1.242 billion**, up **26% year over year**. [[1, 2]]

- **Royalty revenue:** **$737 million**, up **27% YoY** from **$580 million** in Q3 fiscal 2025. [[2]]
- **License and other revenue:** **$505 million**, up **25% YoY** from **$403 million**. [[2]]
- Royalty revenue represented roughly **59.3%** of quarterly revenue, while license and other revenue represented roughly **40.7%**. [[2]]
- Arm attributed royalty growth to adoption of higher-royalty-rate technologies—including **Armv9** and **Arm Compute Subsystems (CSS)**—as well as rising deployment of Arm chips in data centers. [[2]]

[[1]] AWS’s fifth-generation Graviton processor, based on the higher-performance **Neoverse CSS V3**, has **192 cores**, double Graviton4’s core count. [[1]] 

The central implication is that the reported $737 million of total royalties was helped by both higher Arm content/value per chip and a rapidly expanding data-center opportunity, but Arm’s Q3 disclosure does **not** separately quantify Neoverse revenue or data-center royalty dollars. [[2]]

tool_arguments.query: Arm Holdings Q1 fiscal 2026 royalty licensing revenue data-center Neoverse

trajectory.content: Arm Holdings Q1 fiscal 2026 royalty licensing revenue data-center Neoverse

Arm’s Q1 FY2026 (quarter ended June 30, 2025; reported July 30, 2025) revenue was **$1.053 billion**, up **12% year over year** and its best first quarter to date. [[1]] [[2]]

- **Royalty revenue:** **$585 million**, up **25% YoY** from **$467 million** in Q1 FY2025. [[1]]
- **License and other revenue:** **$468 million**, down **1% YoY** from **$472 million**, which Arm attributed to normal timing and size variation in high-value license agreements and backlog contributions. [[1]]
- **License pipeline indicator:** annualized contract value was **$1.528 billion**, up **28% YoY**, while remaining performance obligations were **$2.232 billion**, up **3% YoY**. [[1]] 

Data-center demand was a stated contributor to royalty growth, alongside Armv9 adoption and the ramp of Arm Compute Subsystems (CSS); Arm did **not** disclose a dollar amount or separate growth rate for data-center royalties in its Q1 FY2026 release. [[1]] 

For **Neoverse**, Arm said it expected Arm Neoverse-based chips’ share at the top hyperscalers to reach **nearly 50% during calendar 2025**, supported by demand for high-performance, energy-efficient cloud and AI compute. [[2]] 

CSS licensing adds an important leading indicator for future royalties: Arm had signed **16 CSS licenses with 10 companies**, more than double the prior-year count; five companies were already shipping CSS-based chips, and Q1 added **three** licenses—**two data-center** and **one PC**. [[1]] 

The key read-through is that FY2026 Q1 growth was royalty-led rather than licensing-led: royalties rose $118 million year over year while licensing declined $4 million, with data-center/Neoverse deployment and higher-value Armv9/CSS content identified as principal drivers. [[1]]

trajectory.content: Equinix Q2 2026 xScale and AI data-center leasing demand revenue figure

**Q2 2026 read-through:** Equinix’s xScale leasing demand was exceptionally strong: it signed **134 MW of xScale leases across the Americas** during Q2, demonstrating substantial hyperscale capacity absorption. [[1]] 

The xScale platform had **604 MW leased** across its current portfolio at quarter-end, versus more than **2,000 MW of total capacity when fully built out**, indicating a large remaining development runway but also meaningful execution, power-availability, and preleasing requirements. [[1]] 

The Hampton transaction was included in the 134 MW and generated approximately **$120 million of non-recurring fees**, which was a material contributor to Q2’s reported **16% year-over-year revenue growth** to **$2.625 billion**. [[2]] [[3]] 

Demand was not limited to xScale: Equinix reported **23% year-over-year annualized gross-bookings growth**, its second-highest volume on record, and a record sold-but-not-yet-installed backlog. [[3]] 

Management also reported that about **30% of remaining 2026 retail expansion capacity had been pre-sold** and that more than **45% of its Q3 bookings target** had already closed, supporting a broader view of tight, accelerating demand across both retail colocation and hyperscale-oriented capacity. [[2]] 

AI is an important demand driver, but Equinix did **not** disclose what portion of the 134 MW xScale signings was specifically AI-related; its formal commentary instead characterized customer demand as broad-based across networking, cloud, and AI infrastructure. [[3]] 

The practical implication is favorable for xScale growth and monetization: Equinix is accelerating more than **7,000 cabinets** that had been scheduled for 2027 into **Q4 2026**, while lifting its full-year revenue-growth guidance to **11%–12%** from **10%–11%**. [[1]] 

Investors should normalize the quarter for the Hampton-related fee, however, because the company explicitly attributed part of Q2 revenue and profit growth to one-time xScale fees rather than recurring leasing revenue. [[3]] [[2]]

Equinix has not yet filed or reported **Q3 2026** as of October 17, 2026: its investor-relations filing page identifies the latest quarterly filing as the **Q2 2026 Form 10-Q**, filed July 29, 2026, while Q3 earnings are scheduled for October 28, 2026. [[1, 2]]

|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|

tool_arguments.query: Equinix Q2 2026 xScale and AI data-center leasing demand revenue figure

trajectory.content: Equinix Q2 2026 xScale and AI data-center leasing demand revenue figure

**Q2 2026 read-through:** Equinix’s xScale leasing demand was exceptionally strong: it signed **134 MW of xScale leases across the Americas** during Q2, demonstrating substantial hyperscale capacity absorption. [[1]] 

The xScale platform had **604 MW leased** across its current portfolio at quarter-end, versus more than **2,000 MW of total capacity when fully built out**, indicating a large remaining development runway but also meaningful execution, power-availability, and preleasing requirements. [[1]] 

The Hampton transaction was included in the 134 MW and generated approximately **$120 million of non-recurring fees**, which was a material contributor to Q2’s reported **16% year-over-year revenue growth** to **$2.625 billion**. [[2]] [[3]] 

Demand was not limited to xScale: Equinix reported **23% year-over-year annualized gross-bookings growth**, its second-highest volume on record, and a record sold-but-not-yet-installed backlog. [[3]] 

Management also reported that about **30% of remaining 2026 retail expansion capacity had been pre-sold** and that more than **45% of its Q3 bookings target** had already closed, supporting a broader view of tight, accelerating demand across both retail colocation and hyperscale-oriented capacity. [[2]] 

AI is an important demand driver, but Equinix did **not** disclose what portion of the 134 MW xScale signings was specifically AI-related; its formal commentary instead characterized customer demand as broad-based across networking, cloud, and AI infrastructure. [[3]] 

The practical implication is favorable for xScale growth and monetization: Equinix is accelerating more than **7,000 cabinets** that had been scheduled for 2027 into **Q4 2026**, while lifting its full-year revenue-growth guidance to **11%–12%** from **10%–11%**. [[1]] 

Investors should normalize the quarter for the Hampton-related fee, however, because the company explicitly attributed part of Q2 revenue and profit growth to one-time xScale fees rather than recurring leasing revenue. [[3]] [[2]]

[[1]] [[2]] 

For xScale specifically, Equinix signed **134 MW** of leases across the Americas in Q2 2026, including the Hampton transaction; this is a megawatt leasing measure, not a stated percentage of company-wide leasing or bookings. [[3]] [[1]] 

The identifiable Q2 revenue contribution was approximately **$120 million of non-recurring xScale leasing fees** from Hampton, equivalent to **4.6% of total Q2 revenue of $2.625 billion**. [[1]] [[2]] 

On the reported revenue bridge, Equinix generated **$2.377 billion of recurring revenue (90.6% of total)** and **$248 million of non-recurring revenue (9.4%)**; the company did not publish an exact xScale/AI split of either total. [[2]] 

Thus, the defensible takeaway is: **AI was described as a major driver of large deals, xScale leasing totaled 134 MW, and the disclosed Hampton xScale fee represented roughly 4.6% of Q2 revenue—but no disclosed AI share of total leasing or revenue exists.** [[1]] [[3]] [[1]] [[2]]

**Q2 2026 read-through:** Equinix’s xScale leasing demand was exceptionally strong: it signed **134 MW of xScale leases across the Americas** during Q2, demonstrating substantial hyperscale capacity absorption. [[1]] 

The xScale platform had **604 MW leased** across its current portfolio at quarter-end, versus more than **2,000 MW of total capacity when fully built out**, indicating a large remaining development runway but also meaningful execution, power-availability, and preleasing requirements. [[1]] 

The Hampton transaction was included in the 134 MW and generated approximately **$120 million of non-recurring fees**, which was a material contributor to Q2’s reported **16% year-over-year revenue growth** to **$2.625 billion**. [[2]] [[3]] 

Demand was not limited to xScale: Equinix reported **23% year-over-year annualized gross-bookings growth**, its second-highest volume on record, and a record sold-but-not-yet-installed backlog. [[3]] 

Management also reported that about **30% of remaining 2026 retail expansion capacity had been pre-sold** and that more than **45% of its Q3 bookings target** had already closed, supporting a broader view of tight, accelerating demand across both retail colocation and hyperscale-oriented capacity. [[2]] 

AI is an important demand driver, but Equinix did **not** disclose what portion of the 134 MW xScale signings was specifically AI-related; its formal commentary instead characterized customer demand as broad-based across networking, cloud, and AI infrastructure. [[3]] 

The practical implication is favorable for xScale growth and monetization: Equinix is accelerating more than **7,000 cabinets** that had been scheduled for 2027 into **Q4 2026**, while lifting its full-year revenue-growth guidance to **11%–12%** from **10%–11%**. [[1]] 

Investors should normalize the quarter for the Hampton-related fee, however, because the company explicitly attributed part of Q2 revenue and profit growth to one-time xScale fees rather than recurring leasing revenue. [[3]] [[2]]

AWS revenue was $42.232 billion, up 37% year over year, while AWS operating income was $16.621 billion versus $10.160 billion a year earlier; the implied/reported segment operating margin was 39.4%. [[1]] [[2]]

**AI contribution:** Amazon did not disclose a separate quarterly dollar revenue or operating-profit contribution from AI within AWS. [[1]] However, management said AWS’s AI business exceeded a **$25 billion annual revenue run rate** and was growing at a **triple-digit year-over-year percentage rate**. [[1]] Amazon also said its chips business—which includes its AI-related infrastructure offerings—exceeded a separate **$25 billion annual revenue run rate**, likewise with triple-digit growth. [[1]] 

At the consolidated level, Amazon reported Q2 operating income of **$27.5 billion**, up from $19.2 billion in Q2 2025, meaning AWS generated roughly 60% of company operating income in the quarter. [[1]] [[2]] Net income of $62.6 billion included **$53.4 billion of non-operating pre-tax other income**, primarily related to Amazon’s Anthropic investment, so that gain should not be interpreted as AWS operating performance or recurring AI operating profit. [[1]]

Microsoft’s latest reported quarter was fiscal Q2 2026, ended December 31, 2025 and released January 28, 2026. [[1]]

- **Azure growth:** Azure and other cloud services revenue grew **39% year over year**, or **38% in constant currency**, versus **40% reported / 39% constant currency** in fiscal Q1 2026. [[1]] [[2]]
- **AI contribution:** Microsoft did **not disclose a separate AI percentage-point contribution** to Azure’s 39% growth in its Q2 materials. It said Azure growth was driven by demand across its services portfolio and continued growth across all workloads, while defining Azure and other cloud services as including cloud and AI consumption-based services. [[3]] [[4]]
- **Broader cloud results:** Intelligent Cloud revenue was **$32.9 billion**, up **29%** year over year, and Microsoft Cloud revenue reached **$51.5 billion**, up **26%**. [[5]]
- **AI demand and constraints:** Management said demand continued to exceed available supply, and noted that efficiency gains in its fungible fleet allowed capacity to be reallocated to monetized Azure demand during the quarter. [[5]]
- **Profitability implication:** Microsoft said Microsoft Cloud gross margin was **67%**, with the year-over-year decline reflecting continuing AI-infrastructure investment and increased AI-product usage, partly offset by Azure and Microsoft 365 efficiency gains. [[5]] 

In short, Azure expanded at a still-exceptional **39% reported growth rate**, but decelerated modestly from Q1; AI is clearly embedded in the growth narrative and infrastructure spending, yet Microsoft did not provide the precise “AI contribution” figure it had disclosed in some earlier periods. [[2]] [[6]]

- **AWS growth:** AWS revenue was **$42.2 billion in Q2 2026**, up **36.7% year over year**—its fastest growth in 18 quarters—and Amazon said the business reached a **$169 billion annualized revenue run rate**. [[1]]

- **Management’s key comment on workload contribution:** Andy Jassy said AWS was seeing strong growth in both **AI** and **non-AI (“core”)** workloads, with each supporting the other rather than AI being an isolated revenue stream. [[2]]

- **Mechanism:** Management said AI adoption encourages customers to move to AWS and increases core-service consumption; moreover, post-training reinforcement learning and AI-agent tool use are largely CPU-intensive, benefiting AWS core compute as well as AI accelerators. [[3]]

- **Important caveat:** Therefore, it would be inaccurate to attribute all—or a defined portion—of the 36.7% AWS growth rate to AI: Amazon disclosed rapid AI revenue growth, but **did not quantify AI’s percentage-point contribution** to Q2 AWS growth. [[3, 1]]

tool_arguments.query: Microsoft Azure Q2 2026 revenue growth AI contribution

trajectory.content: Microsoft Azure Q2 2026 revenue growth AI contribution

Microsoft’s latest reported quarter was fiscal Q2 2026, ended December 31, 2025 and released January 28, 2026. [[1]]

- **Azure growth:** Azure and other cloud services revenue grew **39% year over year**, or **38% in constant currency**, versus **40% reported / 39% constant currency** in fiscal Q1 2026. [[1]] [[2]]
- **AI contribution:** Microsoft did **not disclose a separate AI percentage-point contribution** to Azure’s 39% growth in its Q2 materials. It said Azure growth was driven by demand across its services portfolio and continued growth across all workloads, while defining Azure and other cloud services as including cloud and AI consumption-based services. [[3]] [[4]]
- **Broader cloud results:** Intelligent Cloud revenue was **$32.9 billion**, up **29%** year over year, and Microsoft Cloud revenue reached **$51.5 billion**, up **26%**. [[5]]
- **AI demand and constraints:** Management said demand continued to exceed available supply, and noted that efficiency gains in its fungible fleet allowed capacity to be reallocated to monetized Azure demand during the quarter. [[5]]
- **Profitability implication:** Microsoft said Microsoft Cloud gross margin was **67%**, with the year-over-year decline reflecting continuing AI-infrastructure investment and increased AI-product usage, partly offset by Azure and Microsoft 365 efficiency gains. [[5]] 

In short, Azure expanded at a still-exceptional **39% reported growth rate**, but decelerated modestly from Q1; AI is clearly embedded in the growth narrative and infrastructure spending, yet Microsoft did not provide the precise “AI contribution” figure it had disclosed in some earlier periods. [[2]] [[6]]

[[2]]
- Management characterized these wins as diverse, generally sub-1-MW/network-oriented deployments, including private-AI and broader service-provider demand, rather than a concentrated large single-customer or single-site lease. [[2]]
- Overall Q2 reported operating revenue was **$1.924 billion**, including **$1.146 billion of rental revenue**, but Digital Realty did **not** identify what share of either figure was generated by AI customers or workloads. [[1]]
- Demand evidence extended beyond the quarter: Digital Realty said it signed two hyperscale leases in July worth **$410 million of annualized GAAP base rent at 100% share** ($205 million at its share), while its Q2-ending backlog reached **$1.9 billion at 100% share** ($1.4 billion at its share). [[1, 3]]

**Bottom line:** AI was a material and growing leasing contributor—about **$22 million of annualized rent implied within the $108 million connected-capacity segment**—but the company’s disclosures do not support treating that figure as Q2 AI revenue or as total AI-related leasing across all Digital Realty product categories. Arm’s Q1 FY2026 (quarter ended June 30, 2025; reported July 30, 2025) revenue was **$1.053 billion**, up **12% year over year** and its best first quarter to date. [[1]] [[2]]

- **License pipeline indicator:** annualized contract value was **$1.528 billion**, up **28% YoY**, while remaining performance obligations were **$2.232 billion**, up **3% YoY**. [[1]]

The key read-through is that FY2026 Q1 growth was royalty-led rather than licensing-led: royalties rose $118 million year over year while licensing declined $4 million, with data-center/Neoverse deployment and higher-value Armv9/CSS content identified as principal drivers. [[1]]

Arm’s Q1 FY2026 (quarter ended June 30, 2025; reported July 30, 2025) revenue was **$1.053 billion**, up **12% year over year** and its best first quarter to date. [[1]] [[2]]

- **Royalty revenue:** **$585 million**, up **25% YoY** from **$467 million** in Q1 FY2025. [[1]]

CSS licensing adds an important leading indicator for future royalties: Arm had signed **16 CSS licenses with 10 companies**, more than double the prior-year count; five companies were already shipping CSS-based chips, and Q1 added **three** licenses—**two data-center** and **one PC**. [[1]]

tool_arguments.query: Super Micro Computer auditor resignation accounting investigation latest development 2026

trajectory.content: Super Micro Computer auditor resignation accounting investigation latest development 2026

**What happened:** Super Micro Computer’s FY2024 Form 10-K, covering the year ended June 30, 2024, was delayed while the company assessed internal controls and while an independent Special Committee investigated concerns involving governance, transparency, and financial-reporting controls raised by its then-auditor, Ernst & Young (EY). [[1]]

**Auditor resignation:** EY resigned on October 24, 2024, and Supermicro disclosed the resignation in an October 30 SEC filing; EY stated that recently received information meant it could no longer rely on management’s and the Audit Committee’s representations and was unwilling to be associated with management-prepared financial statements. [[1]] [[2]]

**Why the review mattered:** The Board’s Special Committee had reported interim findings to EY on October 2, but Supermicro said EY resigned before the review was complete and before the committee had obtained all relevant information. [[1]]

**Replacement auditor and investigation outcome:** The Audit Committee appointed BDO USA as EY’s replacement on November 18, 2024, while the Special Committee’s review—supported by independent counsel and forensic accountants—ultimately took more than three months. [[1]] [[3]] The company later said the Special Committee found EY’s resignation conclusions were not supported by the facts examined in the review. [[3]]

**10-K resolution:** Supermicro filed its delayed FY2024 10-K, plus the outstanding Q1 and Q2 FY2025 10-Qs, on February 25, 2025; it said no previously filed financial statements were restated and Nasdaq notified the company that it had regained compliance with its filing requirement. [[4]] [[5]]

**Important qualification:** Filing the 10-K and avoiding a restatement resolved the reporting delinquency, but it did not mean the company’s control environment was clean: BDO’s audit opinion said the FY2024 financial statements were fairly presented, while BDO issued an adverse opinion on Supermicro’s internal control over financial reporting as of June 30, 2024. [[6]]

**Bottom line:** The sequence was a serious governance-and-controls event—not a confirmed historical financial-statement restatement: EY’s unusually forceful exit intensified the issue, the company conducted a special investigation and changed auditors, and it eventually became current with SEC and Nasdaq reporting requirements, but the FY2024 control weaknesses remained a material investor-risk consideration. [[2]] [[4]] [[6]]

trajectory.content: Super Micro Computer AI server revenue Q1 fiscal 2027 quarterly results

Super Micro Computer (SMCI) did **not separately disclose an “AI server revenue” dollar line item** in its Q3 fiscal 2026 release; therefore, the reported company-wide net-sales figure is the definitive quarterly revenue measure. [[1]] 

For the fiscal third quarter ended **March 31, 2026**, Supermicro reported net sales of **$10.243 billion**, up **123% year over year** from **$4.600 billion** in Q3 FY2025 and down about **19% sequentially** from **$12.7 billion** in Q2 FY2026. [[1]] 

AI-related platforms reportedly represented **more than 90% of revenue in recent quarters**, which would imply an AI-platform revenue run rate of **more than roughly $9.2 billion** when applied to Q3’s $10.243 billion total; however, that is an inference rather than a company-reported Q3 AI-server-revenue figure. [[2]] [[1]] 

Other Q3 FY2026 results were **GAAP net income of $483 million**, **GAAP diluted EPS of $0.72**, **non-GAAP diluted EPS of $0.84**, and **GAAP gross margin of 9.9%**. [[1]] 

Management attributed the quarterly revenue shortfall versus its prior quarter to customer data-center/site-readiness delays and industry-wide supply constraints, while indicating that it expected delayed revenue to be recognized in subsequent quarters. [[3]] [[4]] 

For Q4 FY2026, Supermicro guided to **$11.0 billion–$12.5 billion** of net sales and maintained FY2026 net-sales guidance of **$38.9 billion–$40.4 billion**. [[1]]

tool_arguments.query: Super Micro Computer auditor resignation accounting investigation latest development 2026

trajectory.content: Super Micro Computer auditor resignation accounting investigation latest development 2026

**What happened:** Super Micro Computer’s FY2024 Form 10-K, covering the year ended June 30, 2024, was delayed while the company assessed internal controls and while an independent Special Committee investigated concerns involving governance, transparency, and financial-reporting controls raised by its then-auditor, Ernst & Young (EY). [[1]]

**Auditor resignation:** EY resigned on October 24, 2024, and Supermicro disclosed the resignation in an October 30 SEC filing; EY stated that recently received information meant it could no longer rely on management’s and the Audit Committee’s representations and was unwilling to be associated with management-prepared financial statements. [[1]] [[2]]

**Why the review mattered:** The Board’s Special Committee had reported interim findings to EY on October 2, but Supermicro said EY resigned before the review was complete and before the committee had obtained all relevant information. [[1]]

**Replacement auditor and investigation outcome:** The Audit Committee appointed BDO USA as EY’s replacement on November 18, 2024, while the Special Committee’s review—supported by independent counsel and forensic accountants—ultimately took more than three months. [[1]] [[3]] The company later said the Special Committee found EY’s resignation conclusions were not supported by the facts examined in the review. [[3]]

**10-K resolution:** Supermicro filed its delayed FY2024 10-K, plus the outstanding Q1 and Q2 FY2025 10-Qs, on February 25, 2025; it said no previously filed financial statements were restated and Nasdaq notified the company that it had regained compliance with its filing requirement. [[4]] [[5]]

**Important qualification:** Filing the 10-K and avoiding a restatement resolved the reporting delinquency, but it did not mean the company’s control environment was clean: BDO’s audit opinion said the FY2024 financial statements were fairly presented, while BDO issued an adverse opinion on Supermicro’s internal control over financial reporting as of June 30, 2024. [[6]]

**Bottom line:** The sequence was a serious governance-and-controls event—not a confirmed historical financial-statement restatement: EY’s unusually forceful exit intensified the issue, the company conducted a special investigation and changed auditors, and it eventually became current with SEC and Nasdaq reporting requirements, but the FY2024 control weaknesses remained a material investor-risk consideration. [[2]] [[4]] [[6]]

tool_arguments.query: Super Micro Computer BDO FY2024 10-K adverse opinion internal control financial reporting

trajectory.content: Super Micro Computer BDO FY2024 10-K adverse opinion internal control financial reporting

**What happened:** Super Micro Computer’s FY2024 Form 10-K, covering the year ended June 30, 2024, was delayed while the company assessed internal controls and while an independent Special Committee investigated concerns involving governance, transparency, and financial-reporting controls raised by its then-auditor, Ernst & Young (EY). [[1]]

**Auditor resignation:** EY resigned on October 24, 2024, and Supermicro disclosed the resignation in an October 30 SEC filing; EY stated that recently received information meant it could no longer rely on management’s and the Audit Committee’s representations and was unwilling to be associated with management-prepared financial statements. [[1]] [[2]]

**Why the review mattered:** The Board’s Special Committee had reported interim findings to EY on October 2, but Supermicro said EY resigned before the review was complete and before the committee had obtained all relevant information. [[1]]

**Replacement auditor and investigation outcome:** The Audit Committee appointed BDO USA as EY’s replacement on November 18, 2024, while the Special Committee’s review—supported by independent counsel and forensic accountants—ultimately took more than three months. [[1]] [[3]] The company later said the Special Committee found EY’s resignation conclusions were not supported by the facts examined in the review. [[3]]

**10-K resolution:** Supermicro filed its delayed FY2024 10-K, plus the outstanding Q1 and Q2 FY2025 10-Qs, on February 25, 2025; it said no previously filed financial statements were restated and Nasdaq notified the company that it had regained compliance with its filing requirement. [[4]] [[5]]

**Important qualification:** Filing the 10-K and avoiding a restatement resolved the reporting delinquency, but it did not mean the company’s control environment was clean: BDO’s audit opinion said the FY2024 financial statements were fairly presented, while BDO issued an adverse opinion on Supermicro’s internal control over financial reporting as of June 30, 2024. [[6]]

**Bottom line:** The sequence was a serious governance-and-controls event—not a confirmed historical financial-statement restatement: EY’s unusually forceful exit intensified the issue, the company conducted a special investigation and changed auditors, and it eventually became current with SEC and Nasdaq reporting requirements, but the FY2024 control weaknesses remained a material investor-risk consideration. [[2]] [[4]] [[6]]

trajectory.content: Marvell Technology data center revenue Q3 fiscal 2026 custom AI silicon and electro-optics

Marvell generated **$1.518 billion of data-center revenue in Q3 fiscal 2026** (three months ended **November 1, 2025**), up **38% year over year** from $1.101 billion and **2% sequentially** from $1.491 billion. [[1]] 

Data center represented **73% of Marvell’s $2.075 billion total Q3 revenue**, making it the company’s dominant end market. [[1]] 

The quarterly increase was approximately **$27.4 million sequentially**, while the year-over-year increase was approximately **$416.8 million**, based on Marvell’s reported end-market revenue figures. [[1]] 

Marvell does **not** disclose separate Q3 revenue amounts for **custom AI silicon** versus **electro-optics**; it reports their contribution within the aggregate data-center end market rather than as standalone product-revenue lines. [[1]] 

Management had identified strong AI demand for both custom silicon and electro-optics as a key growth driver entering Q3, and stated that custom-AI design activity had reached an all-time high, with more than 50 opportunities across over 10 customers. [[2]] 

Total Q3 revenue of **$2.075 billion** exceeded the midpoint of Marvell’s prior **$2.060 billion ±5%** guidance by **$15 million**, while the company guided Q4 fiscal 2026 revenue to **$2.200 billion ±5%**. [[1]] [[2]] [[1]]

tool_arguments.query: Marvell Technology fiscal year end month

trajectory.content: Marvell Technology fiscal year end month

Marvell Technology’s fiscal year ends on the **Saturday nearest January 31**; it is a 52- or 53-week fiscal year, with a 53rd week occurring about every fifth or sixth year. [[1]] 

For example, **FY2025 ended Saturday, February 1, 2025**. [[2]] [[1]] 

Its fiscal quarters are therefore generally: 
- **Q1:** early February through early May 
- **Q2:** early May through early August 
- **Q3:** early August through early November 
- **Q4:** early November through the fiscal year-end Saturday nearest January 31. [[2]] 

For FY2026, the reported quarter-end dates were **May 3, 2025 (Q1)**, **August 2, 2025 (Q2)**, and **November 1, 2025 (Q3)**; Q4 ends at the subsequent fiscal year-end. [[2]]

trajectory.content: Marvell Technology FY2026 full year data center revenue custom AI silicon electro-optics

**Marvell Technology — Q2 FY2026 (quarter ended August 2, 2025):** total revenue reached a record **$2.006 billion**, up **58% year over year** and **6% sequentially**; GAAP diluted EPS was **$0.22** and non-GAAP diluted EPS was **$0.67**. [[1]]

**Data center was the core growth engine:** revenue was **$1.491 billion**, representing **74% of company revenue**, up **69% year over year** and **3% sequentially** from $1.441 billion in Q1 FY2026. [[2]]

**Custom AI silicon and electro-optics:** management identified strong AI demand for these two product categories as a principal driver of the quarter’s growth, and stated that custom-AI design activity had reached an all-time high, with **more than 50 new opportunities across more than 10 customers**. [[2, 3]] 

Marvell did **not** disclose separate Q2 revenue amounts for custom AI silicon versus electro-optics; rather, it stated on the earnings call that the two product lines together accounted for **more than three quarters of data-center revenue**, implying more than roughly **$1.1 billion** of the $1.491 billion data-center total. [[4, 2]] 

For Q3 FY2026, Marvell guided total revenue to **$2.060 billion ±5%**; management expected overall data-center revenue to be approximately flat sequentially, as electro-optics strength offsets a near-term decline in custom revenue, while expecting custom-business growth to become substantially stronger in Q4. [[2, 4]]

**Bottom line:** Q2 demonstrated that Marvell’s AI exposure is already highly material—data center supplied nearly three quarters of revenue and its custom/optical franchises comprised the majority of that segment—but the Q3 outlook also illustrates that custom-silicon ramps can be nonlinear and customer-program timing can create quarterly volatility. [[2, 4]]

trajectory.content:
**Equinix – Revenue & AI-Driven Leasing Demand (as of latest reported periods)**  

| Metric | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Q3 2026 revenue guidance midpoint | **$2.55 B** (9–11% YoY reported growth) | [S1.1, S1.2] |
| Q2 2026 revenue (actual) | **$2.625 B** (+16% YoY) | [S1.2, S1.6] |
| xScale leasing signed in Q2 2026 (Americas) | **134 MW** (total xScale leased **604 MW**) | [S1.5] |
| Annualized gross bookings (Q2 2026) | **$424 M** (+23% YoY) | [S1.2] |
| Net interconnections added (Q2 2026) | **9,700** (record) | [S1.2] |
| Hampton xScale transaction non‑recurring fees (Q2 2026) | **~$120 M** | [S1.2, S1.6] |
| AI model providers / neoclouds using Equinix platform | **8 of top 10 AI model providers; 8 of top 10 neoclouds** | [S1.4] |
| FY 2028 revenue projection (analyst estimate) | **~$10.8 B** (~14% CAGR from 2026 guidance) | [S1.1] |

**Key take‑aways**

- Equinix’s near‑term revenue is guided at ~$2.55 B for Q3 2026, with Q2 already delivering ~$2.63 B and 16% YoY growth driven in part by one‑time xScale fees ($120 M from the Hampton deal).  
- xScale leasing is a concrete AI/hyperscale demand signal: 134 MW signed in Q2 and a total portfolio of 604 MW leased, backed by >$23 B of investment and capacity for ~2,000 MW when fully built out.

tool_arguments.query: Arm Holdings fiscal Q1 fiscal 2026 data center Neoverse royalty revenue

trajectory.content: Arm Holdings fiscal Q1 fiscal 2026 data center Neoverse royalty revenue

Arm’s Q1 FY2026 (quarter ended June 30, 2025; reported July 30, 2025) revenue was **$1.053 billion**, up **12% year over year** and its best first quarter to date. [[1]] [[2]]

- **Royalty revenue:** **$585 million**, up **25% YoY** from **$467 million** in Q1 FY2025. [[1]]
- **License and other revenue:** **$468 million**, down **1% YoY** from **$472 million**, which Arm attributed to normal timing and size variation in high-value license agreements and backlog contributions. [[1]]
- **License pipeline indicator:** annualized contract value was **$1.528 billion**, up **28% YoY**, while remaining performance obligations were **$2.232 billion**, up **3% YoY**. [[1]] 

Data-center demand was a stated contributor to royalty growth, alongside Armv9 adoption and the ramp of Arm Compute Subsystems (CSS); Arm did **not** disclose a dollar amount or separate growth rate for data-center royalties in its Q1 FY2026 release. [[1]] 

For **Neoverse**, Arm said it expected Arm Neoverse-based chips’ share at the top hyperscalers to reach **nearly 50% during calendar 2025**, supported by demand for high-performance, energy-efficient cloud and AI compute. [[2]] 

CSS licensing adds an important leading indicator for future royalties: Arm had signed **16 CSS licenses with 10 companies**, more than double the prior-year count; five companies were already shipping CSS-based chips, and Q1 added **three** licenses—**two data-center** and **one PC**. [[1]] 

The key read-through is that FY2026 Q1 growth was royalty-led rather than licensing-led: royalties rose $118 million year over year while licensing declined $4 million, with data-center/Neoverse deployment and higher-value Armv9/CSS content identified as principal drivers. [[1]]

trajectory.content: Equinix Q2 2026 AI-related data-center leasing xScale demand revenue figure

**Q2 2026 read-through:** Equinix’s xScale leasing demand was exceptionally strong: it signed **134 MW of xScale leases across the Americas** during Q2, demonstrating substantial hyperscale capacity absorption. [[1]] 

The xScale platform had **604 MW leased** across its current portfolio at quarter-end, versus more than **2,000 MW of total capacity when fully built out**, indicating a large remaining development runway but also meaningful execution, power-availability, and preleasing requirements. [[1]] 

The Hampton transaction was included in the 134 MW and generated approximately **$120 million of non-recurring fees**, which was a material contributor to Q2’s reported **16% year-over-year revenue growth** to **$2.625 billion**. [[2]] [[3]] 

Demand was not limited to xScale: Equinix reported **23% year-over-year annualized gross-bookings growth**, its second-highest volume on record, and a record sold-but-not-yet-installed backlog. [[3]] 

Management also reported that about **30% of remaining 2026 retail expansion capacity had been pre-sold** and that more than **45% of its Q3 bookings target** had already closed, supporting a broader view of tight, accelerating demand across both retail colocation and hyperscale-oriented capacity. [[2]] 

AI is an important demand driver, but Equinix did **not** disclose what portion of the 134 MW xScale signings was specifically AI-related; its formal commentary instead characterized customer demand as broad-based across networking, cloud, and AI infrastructure. [[3]] 

The practical implication is favorable for xScale growth and monetization: Equinix is accelerating more than **7,000 cabinets** that had been scheduled for 2027 into **Q4 2026**, while lifting its full-year revenue-growth guidance to **11%–12%** from **10%–11%**. [[1]] 

Investors should normalize the quarter for the Hampton-related fee, however, because the company explicitly attributed part of Q2 revenue and profit growth to one-time xScale fees rather than recurring leasing revenue. [[3]] [[2]]

trajectory.content: Equinix Q2 2026 AI-related data-center leasing xScale demand revenue figure

**Q2 2026 read-through:** Equinix’s xScale leasing demand was exceptionally strong: it signed **134 MW of xScale leases across the Americas** during Q2, demonstrating substantial hyperscale capacity absorption. [[1]] 

The xScale platform had **604 MW leased** across its current portfolio at quarter-end, versus more than **2,000 MW of total capacity when fully built out**, indicating a large remaining development runway but also meaningful execution, power-availability, and preleasing requirements. [[1]] 

The Hampton transaction was included in the 134 MW and generated approximately **$120 million of non-recurring fees**, which was a material contributor to Q2’s reported **16% year-over-year revenue growth** to **$2.625 billion**. [[2]] [[3]] 

Demand was not limited to xScale: Equinix reported **23% year-over-year annualized gross-bookings growth**, its second-highest volume on record, and a record sold-but-not-yet-installed backlog. [[3]] 

Management also reported that about **30% of remaining 2026 retail expansion capacity had been pre-sold** and that more than **45% of its Q3 bookings target** had already closed, supporting a broader view of tight, accelerating demand across both retail colocation and hyperscale-oriented capacity. [[2]] 

AI is an important demand driver, but Equinix did **not** disclose what portion of the 134 MW xScale signings was specifically AI-related; its formal commentary instead characterized customer demand as broad-based across networking, cloud, and AI infrastructure. [[3]] 

The practical implication is favorable for xScale growth and monetization: Equinix is accelerating more than **7,000 cabinets** that had been scheduled for 2027 into **Q4 2026**, while lifting its full-year revenue-growth guidance to **11%–12%** from **10%–11%**. [[1]] 

Investors should normalize the quarter for the Hampton-related fee, however, because the company explicitly attributed part of Q2 revenue and profit growth to one-time xScale fees rather than recurring leasing revenue. [[3]] [[2]]

tool_arguments.query: Equinix Q2 2026 AI-related data-center leasing xScale demand revenue figure

trajectory.content: Equinix Q2 2026 AI-related data-center leasing xScale demand revenue figure

**Q2 2026 read-through:** Equinix’s xScale leasing demand was exceptionally strong: it signed **134 MW of xScale leases across the Americas** during Q2, demonstrating substantial hyperscale capacity absorption. [[1]] 

The xScale platform had **604 MW leased** across its current portfolio at quarter-end, versus more than **2,000 MW of total capacity when fully built out**, indicating a large remaining development runway but also meaningful execution, power-availability, and preleasing requirements. [[1]] 

The Hampton transaction was included in the 134 MW and generated approximately **$120 million of non-recurring fees**, which was a material contributor to Q2’s reported **16% year-over-year revenue growth** to **$2.625 billion**. [[2]] [[3]] 

Demand was not limited to xScale: Equinix reported **23% year-over-year annualized gross-bookings growth**, its second-highest volume on record, and a record sold-but-not-yet-installed backlog. [[3]] 

Management also reported that about **30% of remaining 2026 retail expansion capacity had been pre-sold** and that more than **45% of its Q3 bookings target** had already closed, supporting a broader view of tight, accelerating demand across both retail colocation and hyperscale-oriented capacity. [[2]] 

AI is an important demand driver, but Equinix did **not** disclose what portion of the 134 MW xScale signings was specifically AI-related; its formal commentary instead characterized customer demand as broad-based across networking, cloud, and AI infrastructure. [[3]] 

The practical implication is favorable for xScale growth and monetization: Equinix is accelerating more than **7,000 cabinets** that had been scheduled for 2027 into **Q4 2026**, while lifting its full-year revenue-growth guidance to **11%–12%** from **10%–11%**. [[1]] 

Investors should normalize the quarter for the Hampton-related fee, however, because the company explicitly attributed part of Q2 revenue and profit growth to one-time xScale fees rather than recurring leasing revenue. [[3]] [[2]]

**Q2 2026 takeaway:** Equinix characterized demand as broad-based and stronger than its prior long-term planning assumptions, with demand split between large enterprises modernizing legacy on-premises infrastructure and net-new AI-native workloads/service providers. [[1]]

- Equinix closed **134 MW of xScale leases** in Q2 2026, including the Hampton transaction, which generated roughly **$120 million of non-recurring fees**. [[1]]
- Management said **“the vast majority” of its largest Q2 deals were driven by AI workloads**, consistent with the prior several quarters. [[1]]

- The strength translated into a capacity-response plan: Equinix added nine projects since April and had **52 projects underway across 33 markets** at quarter-end. [[2]]

Equinix generated FY2025 revenue of **$9.217 billion**, up **5% year over year as reported** and **6% on a normalized, constant-currency basis**, for the year ended December 31, 2025. [[1]] 

Its xScale hyperscale/AI platform had **more than 430 MW leased** across **23 operational facilities in 13 metros** at Q4 2025; Equinix also delivered **more than 90 MW of xScale capacity during 2025**. [[2]] [[3]] 

The reported xScale leasing figure is platform-wide leased power capacity rather than a separately disclosed FY2025 AI-only leasing subtotal. [[2]] [[4]]

Related coverage:
**Bottom line:** Federal Reserve tightening is generally a valuation headwind for data-center REITs, while easing is generally supportive, because policy-rate surprises have historically had economically meaningful negative effects on equity REIT prices; one study estimates an unexpected 25-basis-point Fed cut is associated with roughly a 2% rise in U.S. equity-REIT prices on average. [[1]]

**The primary valuation channel is the required return.** A data-center REIT’s enterprise value is commonly framed as stabilized property NOI divided by a cap rate, or as the present value of future cash flows discounted at a required return; higher risk-free rates and often wider credit/equity risk premiums raise those required returns, pushing values lower if NOI is unchanged. [[2]] [[1]]

**Cap-rate sensitivity is especially material because the sector begins from low yields.** Data-center REITs were reported at an implied cap rate of about 4.4% in 2025, the lowest among major REIT property sectors; holding NOI constant, a 50-basis-point move from 4.4% to 4.9% reduces the simple NOI/cap-rate value by about 10.2%. [[3]] [[4]]

**Rates also affect the cost and availability of growth capital.**

**Q2 2026 takeaway:** Equinix characterized demand as broad-based and stronger than its prior long-term planning assumptions, with demand split between large enterprises modernizing legacy on-premises infrastructure and net-new AI-native workloads/service providers. [[1]]

- Equinix closed **134 MW of xScale leases** in Q2 2026, including the Hampton transaction, which generated roughly **$120 million of non-recurring fees**. [[1]]
- Management said **“the vast majority” of its largest Q2 deals were driven by AI workloads**, consistent with the prior several quarters. [[1]]
- Importantly, the company did **not** disclose that all 134 MW of xScale leasing was AI-specific; the more supportable reading is that AI is a major demand accelerant across its portfolio, while xScale leasing activity includes hyperscale capacity transactions such as Hampton. [[1]]
- The strength translated into a capacity-response plan: Equinix added nine projects since April and had **52 projects underway across 33 markets** at quarter-end. [[2]]
- Q2 revenue was **$2.625 billion**, up **16% year over year**, with growth aided by underlying execution and one-time xScale fees. [[3]]
- Management’s practical demand signal was raised outlook and an accelerated expansion program, with long-term annual capex envisioned at **$5 billion–$7 billion**, excluding real-estate acquisitions and xScale. [[1]]

**Bottom line:** The transcript supports a bullish AI-led leasing thesis—AI drove most large deals and is helping sustain capacity demand—but it does not support equating the full 134 MW of Q2 xScale leases directly to AI demand. [[1]]

trajectory.content: Marvell Technology data-center revenue Q3 fiscal 2027 custom AI silicon electro-optics

Marvell had **not yet reported Q3 fiscal 2027 data-center revenue** as of its latest reported quarter; Q2 FY2027 ended August 1, 2026, and data-center revenue was **$2.172 billion**, up **46% year over year** and **18% sequentially**, representing **79%** of total revenue. [[1]] 

For Q3 FY2027, Marvell guided total company revenue to roughly **$3.15 billion** (±5%), while an industry analysis estimated data-center revenue would rise about **20% sequentially** and **75% year over year**; applying 20% to Q2’s $2.172 billion implies approximately **$2.61 billion** in Q3 data-center revenue. [[2]] [[1]] 

The expected Q3 step-up reflects broad data-center demand, with management specifically citing strong connectivity demand and a **significant acceleration in Custom silicon beginning in the second half of FY2027**. [[1]] 

Marvell does **not** disclose quarterly revenue separately for custom AI silicon versus electro-optics in its reported end-market table; however, its FY2026 investor materials characterize optical interconnect as roughly **half of data-center revenue** and custom silicon as approximately **25%** of data-center revenue. [[3]] 

A third-party model estimated Q2 FY2027 electro-optical-component revenue at approximately **$1.4 billion**, up **97.2% year over year**, indicating that optics remained the larger near-term AI revenue contributor even as custom silicon began to accelerate. [[2]] 

The relevant product set includes 800G and 1.6T scale-out optics, NPO/CPO scale-up optical solutions, data-center interconnect modules, and custom XPU/XPU-attach solutions. [[4]]

tool_arguments.query: Marvell Technology carrier enterprise networking revenue Q2 FY2027

trajectory.content: Marvell Technology carrier enterprise networking revenue Q2 FY2027

Marvell’s last separately reported end-market revenue was in **Q3 FY2026** (three months ended November 1, 2025): **enterprise networking revenue was $237.2 million** and **carrier-infrastructure revenue was $167.8 million**. [[1]] 

Those amounts represented **11%** and **8%**, respectively, of Marvell’s $2.075 billion total quarterly revenue. [[1]] 

Versus Q3 FY2025, enterprise networking rose **57%** from $150.9 million, while carrier infrastructure rose **98%** from $84.7 million. [[1]] 

Marvell began combining enterprise networking, carrier infrastructure, consumer, and automotive/industrial into a single **“communications and other”** end market beginning in Q4 FY2026, so subsequent filings do not provide the two requested revenue figures separately. [[1]] 

For context, in the latest reported quarter, Q2 FY2027 ended August 1, 2026, Communications and other revenue was **$567.8 million**, up 10% year over year and down 3% sequentially; this is not directly comparable to the former two-category sum because it includes the additional end markets. [[2]]

Marvell had **not yet reported Q3 fiscal 2027 data-center revenue** as of its latest reported quarter; Q2 FY2027 ended August 1, 2026, and data-center revenue was **$2.172 billion**, up **46% year over year** and **18% sequentially**, representing **79%** of total revenue. [[1]] 

For Q3 FY2027, Marvell guided total company revenue to roughly **$3.15 billion** (±5%), while an industry analysis estimated data-center revenue would rise about **20% sequentially** and **75% year over year**; applying 20% to Q2’s $2.172 billion implies approximately **$2.61 billion** in Q3 data-center revenue. [[2]] [[1]] 

The expected Q3 step-up reflects broad data-center demand, with management specifically citing strong connectivity demand and a **significant acceleration in Custom silicon beginning in the second half of FY2027**. [[1]] 

Marvell does **not** disclose quarterly revenue separately for custom AI silicon versus electro-optics in its reported end-market table; however, its FY2026 investor materials characterize optical interconnect as roughly **half of data-center revenue** and custom silicon as approximately **25%** of data-center revenue. [[3]] 

A third-party model estimated Q2 FY2027 electro-optical-component revenue at approximately **$1.4 billion**, up **97.2% year over year**, indicating that optics remained the larger near-term AI revenue contributor even as custom silicon began to accelerate. [[2]] 

The relevant product set includes 800G and 1.6T scale-out optics, NPO/CPO scale-up optical solutions, data-center interconnect modules, and custom XPU/XPU-attach solutions. [[4]]

trajectory.content: Marvell Q2 FY2027 custom AI silicon revenue figure electro-optics revenue breakdown

**Marvell Technology — Q2 FY2026 (quarter ended August 2, 2025):** total revenue reached a record **$2.006 billion**, up **58% year over year** and **6% sequentially**; GAAP diluted EPS was **$0.22** and non-GAAP diluted EPS was **$0.67**. [[1]]

**Data center was the core growth engine:** revenue was **$1.491 billion**, representing **74% of company revenue**, up **69% year over year** and **3% sequentially** from $1.441 billion in Q1 FY2026. [[2]]

**Custom AI silicon and electro-optics:** management identified strong AI demand for these two product categories as a principal driver of the quarter’s growth, and stated that custom-AI design activity had reached an all-time high, with **more than 50 new opportunities across more than 10 customers**. [[2, 3]] 

Marvell did **not** disclose separate Q2 revenue amounts for custom AI silicon versus electro-optics; rather, it stated on the earnings call that the two product lines together accounted for **more than three quarters of data-center revenue**, implying more than roughly **$1.1 billion** of the $1.491 billion data-center total. [[4, 2]] 

For Q3 FY2026, Marvell guided total revenue to **$2.060 billion ±5%**; management expected overall data-center revenue to be approximately flat sequentially, as electro-optics strength offsets a near-term decline in custom revenue, while expecting custom-business growth to become substantially stronger in Q4. [[2, 4]]

**Bottom line:** Q2 demonstrated that Marvell’s AI exposure is already highly material—data center supplied nearly three quarters of revenue and its custom/optical franchises comprised the majority of that segment—but the Q3 outlook also illustrates that custom-silicon ramps can be nonlinear and customer-program timing can create quarterly volatility. [[2, 4]]

trajectory.content: Marvell Q2 FY2027 custom AI silicon revenue figure electro-optics revenue breakdown

**Marvell Technology — Q2 FY2026 (quarter ended August 2, 2025):** total revenue reached a record **$2.006 billion**, up **58% year over year** and **6% sequentially**; GAAP diluted EPS was **$0.22** and non-GAAP diluted EPS was **$0.67**. [[1]]

**Data center was the core growth engine:** revenue was **$1.491 billion**, representing **74% of company revenue**, up **69% year over year** and **3% sequentially** from $1.441 billion in Q1 FY2026. [[2]]

**Custom AI silicon and electro-optics:** management identified strong AI demand for these two product categories as a principal driver of the quarter’s growth, and stated that custom-AI design activity had reached an all-time high, with **more than 50 new opportunities across more than 10 customers**. [[2, 3]] 

Marvell did **not** disclose separate Q2 revenue amounts for custom AI silicon versus electro-optics; rather, it stated on the earnings call that the two product lines together accounted for **more than three quarters of data-center revenue**, implying more than roughly **$1.1 billion** of the $1.491 billion data-center total. [[4, 2]] 

For Q3 FY2026, Marvell guided total revenue to **$2.060 billion ±5%**; management expected overall data-center revenue to be approximately flat sequentially, as electro-optics strength offsets a near-term decline in custom revenue, while expecting custom-business growth to become substantially stronger in Q4. [[2, 4]]

**Bottom line:** Q2 demonstrated that Marvell’s AI exposure is already highly material—data center supplied nearly three quarters of revenue and its custom/optical franchises comprised the majority of that segment—but the Q3 outlook also illustrates that custom-silicon ramps can be nonlinear and customer-program timing can create quarterly volatility. [[2, 4]]

The transaction closed on **August 14, 2025**, after receiving required regulatory approvals. [[2]] [[3]] 

The disposed business was expected to generate **$225 million–$250 million of FY2026 revenue**, implying an enterprise-value-to-forward-revenue valuation of roughly **10.0x–11.1x**. [[1]] [[2]]

Infineon said the acquired business had approximately **$4 billion of design-win pipeline through 2030**, expected calendar-2025 revenue of **$225 million–$250 million**, and a gross margin of about **60%**; it funded the acquisition with existing liquidity plus additional debt capital. [[3]]

trajectory.content: Super Micro Computer latest revenue guidance fiscal 2027 or fiscal 2026

Super Micro Computer (SMCI) did **not separately disclose an “AI server revenue” dollar line item** in its Q3 fiscal 2026 release; therefore, the reported company-wide net-sales figure is the definitive quarterly revenue measure. [[1]] 

For the fiscal third quarter ended **March 31, 2026**, Supermicro reported net sales of **$10.243 billion**, up **123% year over year** from **$4.600 billion** in Q3 FY2025 and down about **19% sequentially** from **$12.7 billion** in Q2 FY2026. [[1]] 

AI-related platforms reportedly represented **more than 90% of revenue in recent quarters**, which would imply an AI-platform revenue run rate of **more than roughly $9.2 billion** when applied to Q3’s $10.243 billion total; however, that is an inference rather than a company-reported Q3 AI-server-revenue figure. [[2]] [[1]] 

Other Q3 FY2026 results were **GAAP net income of $483 million**, **GAAP diluted EPS of $0.72**, **non-GAAP diluted EPS of $0.84**, and **GAAP gross margin of 9.9%**. [[1]] 

Management attributed the quarterly revenue shortfall versus its prior quarter to customer data-center/site-readiness delays and industry-wide supply constraints, while indicating that it expected delayed revenue to be recognized in subsequent quarters. [[3]] [[4]] 

For Q4 FY2026, Supermicro guided to **$11.0 billion–$12.5 billion** of net sales and maintained FY2026 net-sales guidance of **$38.9 billion–$40.4 billion**. [[1]]

Arm’s Q2 fiscal 2026, ended September 30, 2025, revenue was $1.135 billion; royalty revenue was a record $620 million, up 21% year over year, while **license and other revenue** was $515 million, up 56% year over year. [[1]] 

Royalty growth reflected higher royalty rates from Armv9 and Arm Compute Subsystems (CSS), as well as greater use of Arm-based chips in data centers. [[1]] 

For Neoverse/data center, Arm said data-center royalties doubled year over year, Neoverse had surpassed 1 billion CPUs deployed, and the Neoverse business more than doubled year over year. [[2]] 

Arm also signed one new CSS license for a data-center customer during the quarter, among three total new CSS licenses. [[3]]

**Marvell Technology — Q2 FY2027 AI/Data-Center read-through:** Marvell reported record Q2 FY2027 revenue of **$2.739 billion** for the quarter ended **August 1, 2026**, up **37% year over year** and **13% sequentially**; GAAP diluted EPS was **$0.33** and non-GAAP diluted EPS was **$0.94**. [[1]]

**Data center was the central driver:** Data-center revenue reached **$2.172 billion**, up **46% YoY** and **18% QoQ**, and represented **79%** of company revenue, versus 74% a year earlier. [[2]] This implies that virtually all of Marvell’s near-term growth thesis is now linked to hyperscale AI infrastructure rather than its communications-and-other businesses. [[2]]

**Guidance moved materially higher:** Management guided Q3 FY2027 revenue to **$3.15 billion ±5%**, which at the midpoint implies roughly **15% sequential growth** and more than **50% YoY growth**; it also raised FY2027 revenue expectations to approximately **$12 billion** and FY2028 expectations to approximately **$18 billion**. [[2]] [[3]] Management expects data-center revenue to grow about **60% in FY2027** and more than **60% in FY2028**. [[4]] [[3]]

**Custom AI silicon is shifting from design-win narrative to revenue ramp:** Marvell said its Custom business should accelerate significantly in the second half of FY2027, with growth coming from both **XPU** programs and **XPU-attach** products, including custom NICs and CXL-related products. trajectory.content: Super Micro Computer Q1 fiscal 2026 revenue guidance FY 2026 outlook

Super Micro Computer (SMCI) did **not separately disclose an “AI server revenue” dollar line item** in its Q3 fiscal 2026 release; therefore, the reported company-wide net-sales figure is the definitive quarterly revenue measure. [[1]] 

For the fiscal third quarter ended **March 31, 2026**, Supermicro reported net sales of **$10.243 billion**, up **123% year over year** from **$4.600 billion** in Q3 FY2025 and down about **19% sequentially** from **$12.7 billion** in Q2 FY2026. [[1]] 

AI-related platforms reportedly represented **more than 90% of revenue in recent quarters**, which would imply an AI-platform revenue run rate of **more than roughly $9.2 billion** when applied to Q3’s $10.243 billion total; however, that is an inference rather than a company-reported Q3 AI-server-revenue figure. Other Q3 FY2026 results were **GAAP net income of $483 million**, **GAAP diluted EPS of $0.72**, **non-GAAP diluted EPS of $0.84**, and **GAAP gross margin of 9.9%**. [[1]] 

Management attributed the quarterly revenue shortfall versus its prior quarter to customer data-center/site-readiness delays and industry-wide supply constraints, while indicating that it expected delayed revenue to be recognized in subsequent quarters. [[3]] [[4]] 

For Q4 FY2026, Supermicro guided to **$11.0 billion–$12.5 billion** of net sales and maintained FY2026 net-sales guidance of **$38.9 billion–$40.4 billion**. [[1]]

Supermicro’s edge/IoT embedded portfolio is organized around compact, fanless, industrial, rackmount and outdoor systems designed to put compute, networking and AI inference near devices and users rather than in a central data center. [[1]]

- **Fanless IoT gateways — E50:** palm-size Intel Atom systems for distributed-network data collection and real-time communications, with fanless operation and up to five GbE LAN ports. [[2]]
- **Ultra-compact fanless servers — E100:** Intel Atom, Celeron or Core-based systems for edge compute/inference; configurations support up to 64 GB RAM and optional DIN-rail mounting. [[2]]
- **Compact fanless industrial servers — E302:** Mini-ITX systems using Intel Atom or Xeon D, with broad I/O, fanless construction and operating temperatures up to –20°C to 60°C. [[2]]
- **Compact/industrial and rackmount edge servers:** Supermicro offers short-depth and rack-oriented systems for remote and embedded workloads, with flexible expansion and add-in-card support. [[3]] [[1]]
- **GPU-capable compact edge servers:** Xeon-based compact systems can support up to one double-width or three single-width GPUs, targeting server-grade local AI inference and demanding edge workloads. [[4]]
- **Outdoor edge systems:** rugged, pole-mounted IP65 platforms for 5G and intelligent-edge deployments, with dust/water resistance, thermal protection, and support for up to three GPU accelerators. [[5]] [[4]] 

Representative applications include multi-access edge computing, industrial automation, machine learning, uCPE, smart retail and medical expert systems; other marketed uses include video surveillance, DVR/NVR, digital signage and point-of-sale. [[6]] [[7]] 

In practical product-selection terms, the E50/E100 family suits low-power gateway and control workloads; E302 suits ruggedized industrial installations; compact GPU systems suit vision/AI inference; and rackmount or outdoor systems suit higher-density telco, 5G and distributed-enterprise deployments. Supermicro’s edge/IoT embedded portfolio is organized around compact, fanless, industrial, rackmount and outdoor systems designed to put compute, networking and AI inference near devices and users rather than in a central data center. [[1]]

- **Fanless IoT gateways — E50:** palm-size Intel Atom systems for distributed-network data collection and real-time communications, with fanless operation and up to five GbE LAN ports. [[2]]

- **GPU-capable compact edge servers:** Xeon-based compact systems can support up to one double-width or three single-width GPUs, targeting server-grade local AI inference and demanding edge workloads. [[4]]

[[2]] [[4]] [[5]]

trajectory.content: Super Micro Computer edge IoT embedded systems revenue Q2 FY2026

Supermicro’s edge/IoT embedded portfolio is organized around compact, fanless, industrial, rackmount and outdoor systems designed to put compute, networking and AI inference near devices and users rather than in a central data center. [[1]]

- **Fanless IoT gateways — E50:** palm-size Intel Atom systems for distributed-network data collection and real-time communications, with fanless operation and up to five GbE LAN ports. [[2]]
- **Ultra-compact fanless servers — E100:** Intel Atom, Celeron or Core-based systems for edge compute/inference; configurations support up to 64 GB RAM and optional DIN-rail mounting. [[2]]
- **Compact fanless industrial servers — E302:** Mini-ITX systems using Intel Atom or Xeon D, with broad I/O, fanless construction and operating temperatures up to –20°C to 60°C. [[2]]
- **Compact/industrial and rackmount edge servers:** Supermicro offers short-depth and rack-oriented systems for remote and embedded workloads, with flexible expansion and add-in-card support. [[3]] [[1]]
- **GPU-capable compact edge servers:** Xeon-based compact systems can support up to one double-width or three single-width GPUs, targeting server-grade local AI inference and demanding edge workloads. [[4]]
- **Outdoor edge systems:** rugged, pole-mounted IP65 platforms for 5G and intelligent-edge deployments, with dust/water resistance, thermal protection, and support for up to three GPU accelerators. [[5]] [[4]] 

Representative applications include multi-access edge computing, industrial automation, machine learning, uCPE, smart retail and medical expert systems; other marketed uses include video surveillance, DVR/NVR, digital signage and point-of-sale. [[6]] [[7]] 

In practical product-selection terms, the E50/E100 family suits low-power gateway and control workloads; E302 suits ruggedized industrial installations; compact GPU systems suit vision/AI inference; and rackmount or outdoor systems suit higher-density telco, 5G and distributed-enterprise deployments. [[2]] [[4]] [[5]]
