[[1, 2]] 
The available analyst consensus was **$2.618 billion**, about **$43 million (1.7%) above** the high end of management’s range and **2.7% above** its midpoint, implying the principal near-term revenue-execution risk was expectations above formal guidance. [[3, 2]]

This is not solely a hyperscaler-compute story: Equinix’s differentiated proposition is neutral, connected infrastructure, and the company stated that eight of the top 10 AI model providers and eight of the top 10 neoclouds use its platform for key networking workloads. [[4]]

trajectory.content: Arm Holdings data center royalty and licensing revenue Neoverse CPU fiscal Q3 fiscal Q4 2025 2026

Arm Holdings’ fiscal Q3 2026 ended **December 31, 2025** and produced record revenue of **$1.242 billion**, up **26% year over year**. [[1, 2]]

- **Royalty revenue:** **$737 million**, up **27% YoY** from **$580 million** in Q3 fiscal 2025. [[2]]
- **License and other revenue:** **$505 million**, up **25% YoY** from **$403 million**. [[2]]
- Royalty revenue represented roughly **59.3%** of quarterly revenue, while license and other revenue represented roughly **40.7%**. [[2]]
- Arm attributed royalty growth to adoption of higher-royalty-rate technologies—including **Armv9** and **Arm Compute Subsystems (CSS)**—as well as rising deployment of Arm chips in data centers. [[2]]

**Data-center / Neoverse takeaways:** Arm did not disclose an absolute dollar figure for data-center or Neoverse revenue, but it stated that **data-center royalty revenue grew at a triple-digit year-over-year rate**. [[2]] Arm also said that **Neoverse CPUs surpassed one billion deployed cores** and that its share among leading hyperscalers is expected to approach **50%**. [[1]] AWS’s fifth-generation Graviton processor, based on the higher-performance **Neoverse CSS V3**, has **192 cores**, double Graviton4’s core count. [[1]] 

The central implication is that the reported $737 million of total royalties was helped by both higher Arm content/value per chip and a rapidly expanding data-center opportunity, but Arm’s Q3 disclosure does **not** separately quantify Neoverse revenue or data-center royalty dollars. [[2]]

Arm’s Q1 FY2026 (quarter ended June 30, 2025; reported July 30, 2025) revenue was **$1.053 billion**, up **12% year over year** and its best first quarter to date. [[1]] [[2]]

CSS licensing adds an important leading indicator for future royalties: Arm had signed **16 CSS licenses with 10 companies**, more than double the prior-year count; five companies were already shipping CSS-based chips, and Q1 added **three** licenses—**two data-center** and **one PC**. [[1]] 

The key read-through is that FY2026 Q1 growth was royalty-led rather than licensing-led: royalties rose $118 million year over year while licensing declined $4 million, with data-center/Neoverse deployment and higher-value Armv9/CSS content identified as principal drivers. [[1]]

Equinix reported Q2 2026 revenue of **$2.625 billion** for the quarter ended June 30, 2026, up **16% year over year** on both a reported and normalized constant-currency basis. [[1]] 

The headline growth included both strong underlying demand and one-time xScale fees: recurring revenue was **$2.377 billion**, versus **$2.143 billion** a year earlier, while non-recurring revenue rose to **$248 million** from **$113 million**. [[1]] 

Thus, recurring revenue grew about **10.9% YoY**, indicating that most of the underlying growth remained robust even excluding the unusually large non-recurring contribution. [[1]] 

AI demand appears to be a meaningful operational driver rather than merely a narrative: annualized gross bookings increased **23% YoY**, backlog reached a record, and Equinix added a record **9,700 net interconnections** in the quarter. [[2]] 

Management said customer demand was broad-based and growing, and specifically positioned Equinix to serve enterprise networking, cloud, and AI-infrastructure requirements. [[2]] 

The key analytical caveat is that the **16%** total-revenue growth rate should not be treated as fully recurring, because the company explicitly attributed part of it to one-time xScale fees; the recurring-revenue trajectory and bookings/interconnection metrics are cleaner indicators of sustained AI-led demand. [[1]] [[2]]

trajectory.content: Equinix Q2 2026 revenue $2.625 billion year-over-year growth AI demand

Equinix reported Q2 2026 revenue of **$2.625 billion** for the quarter ended June 30, 2026, up **16% year over year** on both a reported and normalized constant-currency basis. [[1]] 

The headline growth included both strong underlying demand and one-time xScale fees: recurring revenue was **$2.377 billion**, versus **$2.143 billion** a year earlier, while non-recurring revenue rose to **$248 million** from **$113 million**. [[1]] 

Thus, recurring revenue grew about **10.9% YoY**, indicating that most of the underlying growth remained robust even excluding the unusually large non-recurring contribution. [[1]] 

AI demand appears to be a meaningful operational driver rather than merely a narrative: annualized gross bookings increased **23% YoY**, backlog reached a record, and Equinix added a record **9,700 net interconnections** in the quarter. [[2]] 

Management said customer demand was broad-based and growing, and specifically positioned Equinix to serve enterprise networking, cloud, and AI-infrastructure requirements. [[2]] 

The key analytical caveat is that the **16%** total-revenue growth rate should not be treated as fully recurring, because the company explicitly attributed part of it to one-time xScale fees; the recurring-revenue trajectory and bookings/interconnection metrics are cleaner indicators of sustained AI-led demand. [[1]] [[2]]

**Equinix’s Q2 2026 xScale leasing was a strong indicator of AI-led hyperscale demand, but the company did not disclose that all 134 MW was AI-specific.** Equinix closed **134 MW of xScale leases** in the quarter, including the Hampton transaction, and reported that the deal contributed approximately **$120 million of non-recurring fees**. [[1]] 

Management said that “the vast majority” of its largest Q2 deals were driven by AI workloads, while characterizing AI as an accelerant to its broader digitization, cloud, connectivity, and sovereignty demand. [[1]] Therefore, the sound interpretation is that the 134 MW leasing result was **materially AI-influenced rather than a disclosed 134-MW AI-only booking figure**. [[1]] 

The financial impact was visible in reported results: Q2 revenue was **$2.625 billion, up 16% year over year**, with the company explicitly attributing part of that growth to one-time xScale fees. [[2]] Excluding xScale leasing fees, Equinix said adjusted EBITDA margin still increased by roughly **150 basis points year over year**, suggesting the underlying retail/interconnection platform was also performing strongly. [[3]] 

For capacity and capital deployment, Equinix said a significant portion of capacity planned for delivery in the remainder of 2026 had already been committed through bookings and presales, while guiding to **$5–$6 billion** of capital expenditure excluding real-estate acquisitions and xScale. [[1]]

tool_arguments.query: Equinix FY 2025 full year revenue and AI xScale leasing

trajectory.content: Equinix FY 2025 full year revenue and AI xScale leasing

Equinix generated FY2025 revenue of **$9.217 billion**, up **5% year over year as reported** and **6% on a normalized, constant-currency basis**, for the year ended December 31, 2025. [[1]] 

Its xScale hyperscale/AI platform had **more than 430 MW leased** across **23 operational facilities in 13 metros** at Q4 2025; Equinix also delivered **more than 90 MW of xScale capacity during 2025**. [[2]] [[3]] 

The reported xScale leasing figure is platform-wide leased power capacity rather than a separately disclosed FY2025 AI-only leasing subtotal. [[2]] [[4]]

Related coverage:
**Equinix (EQIX) dividend:** the current quarterly common-stock dividend is **$5.16 per share**, a 10% increase, payable March 18, 2026 to shareholders of record February 25, 2026. [[1]] 
Annualizing that rate implies **$20.64 per share**, subject to future board declarations. [[1]] 

For comparison, Equinix distributed **$4.69 per share per quarter**, or **$18.76 annualized**, during 2025. [[2]]

**REIT payout:** a REIT must distribute at least **90% of REIT taxable income**—calculated before the dividends-paid deduction and excluding net capital gains—to preserve REIT qualification; this is a tax-income test, not an AFFO payout-ratio target. [[3]] [[4]] 

Using Equinix’s 2026 guidance, expected cash dividends of approximately **$2.036 billion** represent about **48.0%–49.0% of guided AFFO** of $4.158–$4.238 billion; on a per-share basis, the $20.64 annualized dividend is about **48.3%–49.2%** of guided diluted AFFO per share of $41.93–$42.74. [[5]] 

Thus, Equinix’s cash dividend is roughly a **48%–49% AFFO payout**, while its legally required REIT distribution percentage is measured against taxable income and is at least 90%. [[5]] [[3]]

The headline growth included both strong underlying demand and one-time xScale fees: recurring revenue was **$2.377 billion**, versus **$2.143 billion** a year earlier, while non-recurring revenue rose to **$248 million** from **$113 million**. [[1]]

Management said customer demand was broad-based and growing, and specifically positioned Equinix to serve enterprise networking, cloud, and AI-infrastructure requirements. [[2]] 

The key analytical caveat is that the **16%** total-revenue growth rate should not be treated as fully recurring, because the company explicitly attributed part of it to one-time xScale fees; the recurring-revenue trajectory and bookings/interconnection metrics are cleaner indicators of sustained AI-led demand. trajectory.content: Equinix FY 2025 full year revenue and AI xScale leasing

Equinix generated FY2025 revenue of **$9.217 billion**, up **5% year over year as reported** and **6% on a normalized, constant-currency basis**, for the year ended December 31, 2025. [[1]] 

Its xScale hyperscale/AI platform had **more than 430 MW leased** across **23 operational facilities in 13 metros** at Q4 2025; Equinix also delivered **more than 90 MW of xScale capacity during 2025**. [[2]] [[3]] 

The reported xScale leasing figure is platform-wide leased power capacity rather than a separately disclosed FY2025 AI-only leasing subtotal. [[2]] [[4]]

Related coverage:
**Equinix (EQIX) dividend:** the current quarterly common-stock dividend is **$5.16 per share**, a 10% increase, payable March 18, 2026 to shareholders of record February 25, 2026. [[1]] 
Annualizing that rate implies **$20.64 per share**, subject to future board declarations. [[1]] 

For comparison, Equinix distributed **$4.69 per share per quarter**, or **$18.76 annualized**, during 2025. [[2]]

**REIT payout:** a REIT must distribute at least **90% of REIT taxable income**—calculated before the dividends-paid deduction and excluding net capital gains—to preserve REIT qualification; this is a tax-income test, not an AFFO payout-ratio target. [[3]] [[4]] 

Using Equinix’s 2026 guidance, expected cash dividends of approximately **$2.036 billion** represent about **48.0%–49.0% of guided AFFO** of $4.158–$4.238 billion; on a per-share basis, the $20.64 annualized dividend is about **48.3%–49.2%** of guided diluted AFFO per share of $41.93–$42.74. [[5]] 

Thus, Equinix’s cash dividend is roughly a **48%–49% AFFO payout**, while its legally required REIT distribution percentage is measured against taxable income and is at least 90%. [[5]] [[3]]

[[1]]

- **Management’s key comment on workload contribution:** Andy Jassy said AWS was seeing strong growth in both **AI** and **non-AI (“core”)** workloads, with each supporting the other rather than AI being an isolated revenue stream. [[2]]

- **Mechanism:** Management said AI adoption encourages customers to move to AWS and increases core-service consumption; moreover, post-training reinforcement learning and AI-agent tool use are largely CPU-intensive, benefiting AWS core compute as well as AI accelerators. [[3]]

- **Important caveat:** Therefore, it would be inaccurate to attribute all—or a defined portion—of the 36.7% AWS growth rate to AI: Amazon disclosed rapid AI revenue growth, but **did not quantify AI’s percentage-point contribution** to Q2 AWS growth. [[3, 1]]

trajectory.content: Marvell Technology data-center revenue Q3 fiscal 2027 custom AI silicon electro-optics

Marvell had **not yet reported Q3 fiscal 2027 data-center revenue** as of its latest reported quarter; Q2 FY2027 ended August 1, 2026, and data-center revenue was **$2.172 billion**, up **46% year over year** and **18% sequentially**, representing **79%** of total revenue. [[1]] 

For Q3 FY2027, Marvell guided total company revenue to roughly **$3.15 billion** (±5%), while an industry analysis estimated data-center revenue would rise about **20% sequentially** and **75% year over year**; applying 20% to Q2’s $2.172 billion implies approximately **$2.61 billion** in Q3 data-center revenue. trajectory.content: Marvell Technology data-center revenue Q3 fiscal 2027 custom AI silicon electro-optics

Marvell had **not yet reported Q3 fiscal 2027 data-center revenue** as of its latest reported quarter; Q2 FY2027 ended August 1, 2026, and data-center revenue was **$2.172 billion**, up **46% year over year** and **18% sequentially**, representing **79%** of total revenue. [[1]] 

For Q3 FY2027, Marvell guided total company revenue to roughly **$3.15 billion** (±5%), while an industry analysis estimated data-center revenue would rise about **20% sequentially** and **75% year over year**; applying 20% to Q2’s $2.172 billion implies approximately **$2.61 billion** in Q3 data-center revenue. [[2]] [[1]] 

The expected Q3 step-up reflects broad data-center demand, with management specifically citing strong connectivity demand and a **significant acceleration in Custom silicon beginning in the second half of FY2027**. [[1]] 

Marvell does **not** disclose quarterly revenue separately for custom AI silicon versus electro-optics in its reported end-market table; however, its FY2026 investor materials characterize optical interconnect as roughly **half of data-center revenue** and custom silicon as approximately **25%** of data-center revenue. [[3]] 

A third-party model estimated Q2 FY2027 electro-optical-component revenue at approximately **$1.4 billion**, up **97.2% year over year**, indicating that optics remained the larger near-term AI revenue contributor even as custom silicon began to accelerate. [[2]] 

The relevant product set includes 800G and 1.6T scale-out optics, NPO/CPO scale-up optical solutions, data-center interconnect modules, and custom XPU/XPU-attach solutions. [[4]]

trajectory.content: Marvell Technology FY2026 custom AI silicon revenue percentage data-center

**Marvell Technology — Q2 FY2026 (quarter ended August 2, 2025):** total revenue reached a record **$2.006 billion**, up **58% year over year** and **6% sequentially**; GAAP diluted EPS was **$0.22** and non-GAAP diluted EPS was **$0.67**. [[1]]

**Data center was the core growth engine:** revenue was **$1.491 billion**, representing **74% of company revenue**, up **69% year over year** and **3% sequentially** from $1.441 billion in Q1 FY2026. [[2]]

**Custom AI silicon and electro-optics:** management identified strong AI demand for these two product categories as a principal driver of the quarter’s growth, and stated that custom-AI design activity had reached an all-time high, with **more than 50 new opportunities across more than 10 customers**. [[2, 3]] 

Marvell did **not** disclose separate Q2 revenue amounts for custom AI silicon versus electro-optics; rather, it stated on the earnings call that the two product lines together accounted for **more than three quarters of data-center revenue**, implying more than roughly **$1.1 billion** of the $1.491 billion data-center total. [[4, 2]] 

For Q3 FY2026, Marvell guided total revenue to **$2.060 billion ±5%**; management expected overall data-center revenue to be approximately flat sequentially, as electro-optics strength offsets a near-term decline in custom revenue, while expecting custom-business growth to become substantially stronger in Q4. [[2, 4]]

**Bottom line:** Q2 demonstrated that Marvell’s AI exposure is already highly material—data center supplied nearly three quarters of revenue and its custom/optical franchises comprised the majority of that segment—but the Q3 outlook also illustrates that custom-silicon ramps can be nonlinear and customer-program timing can create quarterly volatility. [[2, 4]]
